Harbor navigation starts with a chart of the channels and a careful look at the tide. The crews of small boats compare the positions of the headland and the old lighthouse before they enter. At the edge of the harbor, fixed marks tell them where the safe water lies.

== Approaching the harbor ==

Charts mark each reef, sand bank and shallow shelf. Sailors look for a light or painted post before changing course. A narrow inlet makes it especially important to confirm a boat's location with two landmarks. The café on the northern bluff is easy to see in daylight, and the lighthouse to the south has a reliable light after dusk.

The entrance is wider on a rising tide. Water moves over the sand and leaves enough room for a short crossing. On a falling tide the crew takes the main channel. A line of foam may reveal the direction of the current when the wind is calm. Wind against the current can turn those small waves into a steep chop.

== Inside the breakwater ==

The jetty reduces the motion of the sea inside the harbor. A flag at the end of the old stone wall warns crews when the landing stage is closed. Visitors can wait on a mooring in the north basin, where the water is deep enough through most of the tide. The harbor office keeps a record of arrivals and departures.

At sunset the harbor's lights gradually become easier to see. Their colors and intervals identify them to anyone who has read the chart. Each pair of lights must be kept in line on a marked approach. A skipper checks both the lights and the depth sounder to avoid relying on a single source of information.

== Departure ==

Fog can build over the water before dawn, especially after a warm night. On those mornings the crew leaves extra time to reach the channel. A short warning signal carries across the basin, but the stones and buildings can make it hard to tell where it came from. Boats move slowly until they have passed both jetties.

The open sea offers a wider path than the harbor entrance, yet the first turn still needs care. A captain clears the last buoy before setting a course along the coast. The crew records the time and the weather in a logbook, where it can help on a future crossing. The chart goes back below deck where the paper can stay dry.
